subject: Math
cluster: B. Tell the number of objects.
text: Count out up to three objects from a larger set, pairing each object with one and only one number name to tell how many.

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can count out up to three objects from a larger set, pairing each object with one and only one number name to tell how many. For example, I can take three blocks from a pile and count them one by one, saying "one, two, three." I know that there are three blocks in total.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can start to count objects from a larger set, but I am still learning how to keep track of which objects I have counted. For example, I can take some marbles from a bag and try to count them, but I might lose track and count the same marble twice. I am still developing my understanding of one-to-one correspondence.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can count out up to three objects from a larger set, but I sometimes forget to say the number name for each object. For example, I can take three crayons from a box and count them, but I might only say "one, two" instead of "one, two, three." I am still learning to connect each object with a number name.

source: Wisconsin Essential Elements (DPI), linked from WI-CC-MATH

subject: Math
text: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than (more) or less than (when the quantities are clearly different) or equal to the number objects in another group.

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can look at two groups of objects and tell you which group has more, less, or the same number of objects. I can use words like "more," "less," and "equal" to describe the number of objects in different groups. I can compare the number of objects in two groups by counting the objects in each group and comparing the numbers. I can use objects to represent the numbers in two groups and compare the quantities.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I am starting to understand the concepts of "more" and "less." I can sometimes identify which group has more objects when the difference is very obvious. I am beginning to use objects to represent numbers. I need support to compare the number of objects in two groups.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can sometimes identify which group has more or less objects, especially when the difference is large. I can use the words "more" and "less" to describe the number of objects in different groups. I can start to compare the number of objects in two groups by counting the objects in each group. I can use objects to represent the numbers in two groups, but I may need help comparing the quantities.

subject: Math
text: Identify shapes as two dimensional or three dimensional

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can identify all basic 2D shapes, including circles, squares, triangles, rectangles, and ovals. I can identify all basic 3D shapes, including spheres, cubes, cones, cylinders, and pyramids. I can explain the difference between 2D and 3D shapes using my own words. descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify some 2D shapes, like circles and squares, but I have trouble with other shapes like triangles and rectangles. I can tell the difference between some 2D and 3D shapes, but I can't always explain why.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Describe and compare measurable attributes.
text: Classify objects according to attributes (e.g., big/small, heavy/light).

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can classify objects according to attributes (big/small, heavy/light). I can, if given a big book and a small book, describe or demonstrate which one is bigger and which one is smaller. I can, if given the shoe of a student and the teacher, identify which one is bigger and which one is smaller. I can, sort heavy and light objects according to weight. I can, if given the hand of a student in the class and the hand of the teacher, identify which one is bigger and which one is smaller. I can, if given two objects of varying weight, describe or demonstrate which is heavy/light or large/small.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can match objects by attribute big and small. I can touch a large object (such as a pumpkin) as teacher describes it as big when compared to a smaller pumpkin toy. I can indicate small pumpkin as teacher describes it as small when compared with a large pumpkin. I can indicate if I want the big ball or the small ball.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can use a model or a template, sort objects by one attribute (big/small or heavy/light). I can sort counting bears by size using a model or template. I can, if given two objects, where one is at least twice the size of the other, identify which one is bigger and which one is smaller with descriptive prompts from the teacher. I can identify bigger ball when shown a beach ball and a tennis ball, and listening to the teacher use voice inflections and kinesthetic motions to exaggerate bigger and smaller. I can identify the bigger ball when shown a golf ball and beach ball and listening to the teacher using voice inflections and motions to exaggerate. I can Sort objects in the classroom into groups of heavy and light (e.g., bowling ball, beach ball, and a rock). I can, if given two pictures of real-life objects, select the bigger one.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand addition as putting together and adding to and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
text: Represent addition as “putting together” or subtraction as “taking from” in everyday activities (e.g., with objects, fingers, sounds, drawings, verbal explanations, or numbers).

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can represent addition as “putting together” or subtraction as “taking from” in everyday activities. I can identify the total number of crayons when one student has three crayons and another student has two, and they put their crayons together to share. Describe the action as put together. I can add to a group of crayons when told to add to group. I can take away from a group of crayons when told to take away from the group. I can given five stickers, give another student one of the five stickers, and describes the action as take away. I can join linking cubes to show action/process of putting together or addition. I can break apart linking cubes/snap blocks/bristle blocks/pop-beads to show action/process of taking from or subtraction.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can put together” or “take from” with teacher. I can together with a teacher add a block to a stack while teacher says, “put together.” I can together with a teacher take a block from a stack while the teacher says, “take away.”
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can follow directions to “put together” by adding one or “take from” by taking one. I can, if given a bowl of counting bears, add a counting bear to the bowl. The teacher calls the action “putting together” or addition. I can take one when the teacher is passing out supplies and directs the students to take one. The teacher calls the action “taking away” or subtraction. I can place popsicle sticks into a circle and use language to describe addition or “putting together”. I can, using cubes, create towers by adding or taking away one cube at a time. I can remove popsicle sticks from a circle and use language to describe subtraction or “taking from”.

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can compare sets of objects and numbers using appropriate vocabulary (more, less, equal). I can when given a four and a six, determine that six is more than four. I can when given two groups of three red counters, determine that they are equal.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can match groups of objects. I can when given two sets of objects match like groups. descriptors.cc_approaching: I can determine equality of sets of objects using appropriate vocabulary (equal). I can when given sets of two bears and two apples, be able to indicate that the sets are equal. I can when given two sets, two of which are equal, be able to indicate the sets that are equal. I can John has three bears and Susie has two bears. John has one more bear than Susie.

subject: Math

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can identify the meaning of the “+” sign (i.e., combine, plus, add), and the “=” sign (equal). I can when given an equation, point to the plus or equal sign in an equation. I can when given three groups of objects (two addends and the sum), identify the “+” sign.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can match the “+” and “=” signs. I can When given a cue, match the plus sign (e.g., The teacher shows a “+” sign and an “=” then points to the “+” sign. descriptors.cc_approaching: I can recognize the “+” and “=” signs. I can When shown a group of symbols, point to/identify the plus/equal sign when prompted by the teacher. I can When shown the plus/equal signs taped on the floor, indicate the sign when prompted by the teacher. I can When shown the plus/equal signs drawn on the board, indicate the sign when prompted by the teacher.
